text.text: Idea Background - explain why your research is important for you / domain (education, medicine, economics).

text:
The first half of the research needed to realize this project helps us understand how sorting and searching algorithms generally work and how to use AI technology to provide accurate, relevant data when given user input. We're interested in pursuing this because it is strongly linked to Software Engineering and, given our curricular program, we believe these studies may increase our chances of survival in the later years. 
The second half of the research involves building website models and UI elements, such as classified lists, search results and product descriptions, which are needed for turning algorithms into practical tools, as well as creating user-friendly experiences. For those of us interested in back-end technology, this is just necessary to study in order to properly plan and test program functionality. For the few of us with experience in designing websites, it helps us understand how to make appealing and informative graphical interfaces.

text.text: Research Question / Problem Statement - describe your problem statement and the question your research aims to answer.

text:
Many ordinary people use music platforms as a way to quickly find pleasant-sounding music through automatically generated playlists and auto-played suggestions, because manually searching for new music involves research about artists and genres that usually takes long amounts of time and experience of listening to various records. People can miss out on art that they would otherwise remember for years to come, just because it's too time-consuming to find information online that would explain their appeal in a way they could understand.
The question we aim to answer is this - Can we make a system that makes it quick and easy for casual listeners to find good music that fits their preferences the closest?

Among the sources and platforms which serve the purpose of finding music include:
general music platforms for searching songs and browsing curated playlists(Spotify, Soundcloud, Bandcamp), AI playlist generators(ChatGPT's AI Playlist Maker, Spotify's AI Playlist Tool, Chosic AI), review magazines(The Rolling Stone, Billboard, Pitchfork), user-written reviewing and rating sites(AlbumOfTheYear, RateYourMusic) and independent reviewers(The Needle Drop).

**

-  The practical value your findings will provide. The problems your work can potentially help to fix. **
Our work consists of creating a website that helps people find favorite songs and albums faster. It does so through an algorithm that recommends the user a list of records matching their written prompt and creates a dedicated page for each respective record, displaying every relevant review, comment, rating or description found online that relates to the original prompt, all in a compact, easy-to-read space. This process makes it simple for music listeners looking to expand their palette, find music fitting of specific events and discover inspirational records they could remember fondly.

To create a superior version of Spotify, we need, I think, to focus on niche yet high-quality music—there is a vast amount of it out there to suit every taste, yet it is missing from Spotify. In this regard, VK Music is miles ahead: there is absolutely no censorship, and the range of music is limited only by copyright restrictions (people even upload lectures by Dugin there).

Furthermore, our project must be completely free for the user (otherwise, we wouldn't be able to give a solid answer to the question of how we intend to lure users away from Spotify and similar services). It could include ads—after all, the project needs a way to sustain itself, and I suspect this will be a topic the mentors raise during the midterm review, given that a viable project cannot exist without revenue. 

The project’s key selling point—the unique feature that sets it apart from competitors—should be a music recommendation and search system that is customizable (offering either deep or superficial control, depending on user preference), efficient, user-friendly, and free from excessive micromanagement. It should help users find music they will enjoy without requiring specialized knowledge of genres or even a clear idea of ​​exactly what they are looking for. Bogdan has already addressed this in the proposal and on the project board and we talked about it a lot.

messages.text: Streaming payouts are distributed pro-rata: a fixed share of revenue divided by each rightsholder's share of total streams (Spotify for Artists). A substantial share of listening is recommendation-guided, so a comparable share of that pool is allocated by placement rather than by deliberate choice. Spotify's own research finds that organic listening is almost always more diverse than algorithmic listening, and that users who grow more generalist move away from algorithmic listening (Anderson et al., WWW '20) — though the authors caution the relationship may not be causal. Placement is decided by interaction history rather than by any description of the music, and because collaborative filtering operates on a matrix in which over 95% of user–item associations are empty, only items that already have listening data can be effectively recommended (Carnovalini et al., 2025). On Radio and Autoplay specifically, Spotify's Discovery Mode lets artists accept a reduced royalty rate for increased likelihood of placement, an arrangement US legislators compared to radio payola in 2021. The effect is not simple homogenisation: a randomised experiment on 853,000 Spotify users found personalised recommendation raised engagement by 28.90% while reducing individual diversity by 11.51% and increasing diversity across listeners by 5.96% (Holtz et al.). What the evidence does establish is that the surfaces allocating the largest share of unchosen listening operate on a representation the listener cannot see, name, or steer

text.text: We need to significantly narrow down our target user group. For over 90% of Spotify’s audience (which totals 777 million users), the platform already provides everything they need: it functions well as a player, its recommendation algorithms suit the vast majority of users, and its actual churn rate is among the lowest in the market—roughly 1.5–2% per month (our previously cited 24.3% figure, derived from Google Play reviews, turned out to be a classic case of survivorship bias). As for the remaining 10% of listeners who aren’t entirely satisfied with Spotify’s features, there is already a wealth of alternatives available. A need for granular control over recommendation algorithms exists only within a very small niche (well under 1%); most people who desire such control can already satisfy their needs by curating streams based on "vibes" or tags—using tools like VK Music, Yandex Music’s "My Wave," or Deezer’s "Flow Tuner"—or by discovering independent music for free via platforms like SoundCloud’s "First Fans" or Bandcamp. Furthermore, we cannot simply build a player with "improved" algorithms on top of Spotify; in November 2024, Spotify permanently closed access to its Audio Features and Recommendations APIs (and by February 2026, it had restricted the test mode to just five users). Consequently, the only legal, cloud-based music sources available to us would be free, open-access databases like Jamendo or FMA, which contain only about 750,000 tracks—most of which are relatively obscure—compared to the 253 million tracks found on major streaming services. The nature of our subject matter inherently implies that, regardless of the niche we choose, we will either face a multitude of well-established, massive competitors or encounter a situation where the audience is too small to justify the high costs of server infrastructure—after all, maintaining complex databases, running backend computations, and handling data traffic for a limited user base is simply not economically viable. In such cases, one is forced to scrape by on donations, advertising, or inflated pricing (which is precisely why AcousticBrainz shut down in 2022, and why a subscription to Roon costs $14.99 per month).

text.text:
"1 percent" is a significant exaggeration. In reality, the number of users who find existing search and recommendation algorithms inadequate is far, far smaller. We face a dilemma: in-depth manual curation of recommendations and support for non-commercial music appeal only to a very narrow niche (well under 1–2% of the market). If we were to build a traditional cloud-based streaming service—complete with our own servers, databases, and a heavy backend—for this handful of users, we would inevitably go bust due to the costs (this is precisely why the AcousticBrainz project shut down in 2022). Here is what we should actually do (this is not just a concept or a proposal):
1) Honestly acknowledge the niche nature of the project (~1% "power users"): We must be clear with our mentor that we are not competing with Spotify for the mass market; rather, we are addressing the fragmentation problem faced by a specific, narrow group. This group might include, for instance, users who maintain personal offline music archives (FLAC files, Bandcamp downloads, soundtracks) or those who search for obscure indie music using acoustic tags—a niche that has been almost entirely hollowed out (especially following the split between Plexamp and TIDAL in October 2024; leaving aside the "vibe-based" search features found on platforms like VK, Yandex, or Deezer, this space is now largely empty). Even so, it is not certain that this group is small enough.
2) Cut server costs to near zero (by adopting a "local-first" or client-side architecture): To ensure the project remains economically viable with a small user base—much like Poweramp or Symfonium—we should shift all resource-intensive computation from the servers to the user's own device. Furthermore, we can provide access to the Jamendo/FMA database as an open, legal sandbox for music discovery, without incurring the costs of hosting the music files ourselves. 3) Frame potential weaknesses as testable hypotheses (I’ve seen this done in another team’s proposal—they openly acknowledged that their intended approach had been tried before and failed, while also noting that many similar, successful projects already exist). Instead of promising an "industry killer," be transparent about risks—such as a limited music catalog or questions regarding monetization (subscriptions vs. one-time purchases/donations)—by including them in your validation and risk assessment sections.

The vast majority of people do not seek out music themselves. They rely on recommendation algorithms or stumble upon new tracks while using TikTok (according to the 2025 TikTok & Luminate Report, 84% of chart-topping tracks first go viral on TikTok). Spotify and other major platforms fully satisfy their needs. 
    Those who curate their playlists more carefully are generally content with the tools provided by Spotify, VK, Deezer (whose "Flow Tuner" feature allows users to toggle genres and moods in real-time), and SoundCloud, or they rely on recommendations from friends and large language models (LLMs). 
    Then there are the more demanding(or perhaps simply old-fashioned) music enthusiasts who invest significant time in actively searching for new music outside of mainstream platforms and LLMs, guided by their own specific tastes and extensive personal playlists (though I suspect even most of them rarely seek out anything truly new). Consequently, the way this problem is framed is inherently misleading: true music enthusiasts have no need for a discovery tool designed for the casual listener.

i guess i can say from experience that review sites are only as good as you trust ratings, and the next best thing is friend recommendations or AI recommendations, but again verifying whether they're good for what you're looking for means listening to what tracks get recommended yourself, and its just a hit-or-miss experience, sometimes you don't get how the songs correlate with what you want. I don't agree with the argument that viral music means good recommendations though. Chart-topping tracks relate to newer music only and they cover a limited number of songs, I don't think its fair to claim that level of exposure makes it as easy to find music which may be released earlier, or is usually longer than 2-3 minutes, or is part of a more specific sound that just isn't as used on TikTok

Its not that music enthusiasts rarely seek out anything new because they don't want to, its because, like you said, it takes a lot of time investment, which i think could be solved so that active searching takes less time. 
I do think its hard to count which kinds of music enjoyers are conservative about their music vs those who want more music like the sort they already like. Some sources(i can't remember which but it was in one article) say that music discovery tendencies show up for most people during their early 20s and fades away in their 30s or 40s, and theres these online forums and communities dedicated to recommending new releases and underrated albums and songs. 
I do think this is a niche topic at the end of the day and the best framing you could make around it is that its something people may occassionally want, but it doesn't hurt them if they can't do it, and theres a minority of people who would probably be interested in it. That's my perspective

text: Problem statement nr. 1(Nikita)

text.text:
Problem: Over 80% of time on the start of making song producer spends on searching in libraries with more than 150 000 files of sounds.
    Modern music producers typically store between 500 GB and 3 TB of audio samples across multiple drives. Over 80% of these files lack accurate metadata or have nondescript filenames (such as Snare_02_processed_v3.wav). Existing desktop catalogers rely on manual tags, freeze when indexing libraries over 150,000 files, or require subscription-based cloud uploads.

text: Problem Statement nr. 2(Andrei)

text.text: The algorithms of music streaming services (i.e Spotify) are repetitive and predictable, promoting familiarity over discoverability by often recommending the same known songs. This hurts both the users, who get fatigued from frequent listening repetition, as well as the small artists who have an extremely difficult time reaching an audience due to the algorithm promoting only the top performing artists.

text: Problem statement nr. 3(Bogdan)

text.text:
Finding samples in music takes too much time for independent producers. Independent hip-hop, electronic and experimental producers find it time-consuming to search for samples in existing records online, as most songs can only be searched by details of the whole record, like genre, style and artist, so they need to listen through them one by one until they find a part they can use.
    Context: Sources like Tracklib, Samplette and Splice exist for this purpose, with only Tracklib and Samplette offering categorization on published records. Tracklib only covers a limited library of licensed music, whereas Samplette's search tool is a random-suggestion button, but they don't provide information about individual sections of a song.

text: Problem Statement nr. 4(me)

text.text: Active listeners who have used streaming services for more than 2–3 years (about 10–15% of the user base) find it easy to discover new music, but as a result, they end up with thousands—sometimes even tens of thousands—of tracks in a single, flat "Liked Songs" list, along with dozens of albums set aside for later. Consequently, 80–90% of their personal collection remains "buried." Platforms like Spotify, YouTube Music, and Yandex Music lack multidimensional filtering for one’s own library—Spotify, for instance, offers only basic, non-combinable genre "chips" at the top of the "Liked Songs" list, which disappear as soon as you start a search. Furthermore, hitting "shuffle" on a list of 10,000+ tracks causes the app to lag, often defaulting to playing only the most recent 50–100 songs. Albums saved for later are easily forgotten, as there is no system for tracking their status (e.g., "to listen to," "currently exploring," or "archived"). It is also impossible to quickly generate a dynamic selection from one’s own curated collection—such as instrumental, mid-tempo tracks perfect for coding or studying—without spending hours manually organizing everything into folders. Neither Google nor ChatGPT has access to a user’s personal library, meaning they cannot filter or play its contents; meanwhile, the once-popular third-party tool SmarterPlaylists ceased to function properly following changes to the Spotify API.

As a result, 80–90% of their library gets buried: platforms lack multidimensional filtering, Shuffle on 10k+ tracks lags and loops the top 50–100 recent songs, and saved albums have no backlog tracking (To Listen / Exploring / Archived).
Target Audience & Sub-groups (10–15% of market = ~80–120M paid users globally per

• Flat-List Hoarders (~45% of TG): dump all genres into Liked Songs, suffer from broken Shuffle and mood whiplash.
• Focused Workers / Coders (~25% of TG): need dynamic slices of their own library (e.g., instrumental + mid-tempo for coding) because editorial playlists like "Deep Focus" are filled with generic Ghost Artist / PFC stock music.
• Album Backloggers (~15% of TG): save 100–300 albums and forget 85% of them due to zero status tracking or notes.
• Cross-Platform Listeners (~10–20% in our region): collection split across Spotify, YouTube Music, and SoundCloud.
• Rule-Based Curators (~5% of TG): power users needing boolean logic (AND/OR/NOT, BPM, last played date).

• Streaming Apps: Spotify genre chips can't be combined, ignore filters on shuffle, and aren't even available in Moldova; desktop BPM/Key columns can't be sorted or filtered. Apple Music still lacks Smart Playlists on iOS. YouTube Music has no genre filters for libraries. Only Yandex Music partially solves the worker case ("My Wave: Favorites + No Words"), but acts as a black-box radio and lacks Western major releases.
• Google & LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini): only do external discovery; they have zero access to a user's personal library, can't control playback, and hallucinate BPM/vocal status on 80% of non-mainstream tracks.
• Specialized AI & Generators: Cyanite.ai is B2B-only, Sonoteller.ai caps free users at 10 tracks/month, and Endel/Mubert generate synthetic audio instead of filtering your own library.
• 3rd-Party Organizers: SmarterPlaylists and Organize Your Music broke when Spotify deprecated Audio Features in Nov 2024. Chosic caps free analysis at 1,000 songs, while Skiley and Playlistation require paid subs and spam your sidebar with static playlists based on coarse artist genres. Marvis Pro (~$10) is iOS + Apple Music only. Record Club requires manual album logging.
• Manual Sorting (Folders / Notion): sorting 3,600 tracks at 10 sec/track takes 10 hours of manual desktop drag-and-drop + 30 min/week maintenance.

Operational, not informational problem: cannot be solved by Googling or prompting ChatGPT (directly passes our mentor's filter).
Low direct competition in 2026: Spotify's API changes killed legacy free tools (SmarterPlaylists), leaving a clear market gap.
Strong local angle: Spotify's basic Liked Songs genre filters aren't even rolled out in Moldova.
Easy Midterm 2 validation: finding 15–20 university students with 2,000+ liked songs for video interviews is super easy.
Buildable Core: DB schema, album backlog kanban, boolean query engine, true stratified shuffle, and LLM Text-to-Filter over tagged metadata are straightforward to build.

"Vitamin vs. Painkiller" (Passive tolerance): 75–85% of listeners are passive, and even among the 10–15% hoarders, many just accept looping their top 50 tracks if onboarding takes too much effort.

text_entities.text: Problem:

Active listeners (2–3+ years on streaming) accumulate 2,000–10,000+ tracks in a flat Liked Songs list and dozens of saved albums. As a result, 80–90% of their library gets buried: platforms lack multidimensional filtering, Shuffle on 10k+ tracks lags and loops the top 50–100 recent songs, and saved albums have no backlog tracking (To Listen / Exploring / Archived).
Target Audience & Sub-groups (10–15% of market = ~80–120M paid users globally per
IFPI 2026

• Flat-List Hoarders (~45% of TG): dump all genres into Liked Songs, suffer from broken Shuffle and mood whiplash.
• Focused Workers / Coders (~25% of TG): need dynamic slices of their own library (e.g., instrumental + mid-tempo for coding) because editorial playlists like "Deep Focus" are filled with generic Ghost Artist / PFC stock music.
• Album Backloggers (~15% of TG): save 100–300 albums and forget 85% of them due to zero status tracking or notes.
• Cross-Platform Listeners (~10–20% in our region): collection split across Spotify, YouTube Music, and SoundCloud.
• Rule-Based Curators (~5% of TG): power users needing boolean logic (AND/OR/NOT, BPM, last played date).
Current Workarounds & Why They Fail:

• Streaming Apps: Spotify genre chips can't be combined, ignore filters on shuffle, and aren't even available in Moldova; desktop BPM/Key columns can't be sorted or filtered. Apple Music still lacks Smart Playlists on iOS. YouTube Music has no genre filters for libraries. Only Yandex Music partially solves the worker case ("My Wave: Favorites + No Words"), but acts as a black-box radio and lacks Western major releases.
• Google & LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini): only do external discovery; they have zero access to a user's personal library, can't control playback, and hallucinate BPM/vocal status on 80% of non-mainstream tracks.
• Specialized AI & Generators: Cyanite.ai is B2B-only, Sonoteller.ai caps free users at 10 tracks/month, and Endel/Mubert generate synthetic audio instead of filtering your own library.
• 3rd-Party Organizers: SmarterPlaylists and Organize Your Music broke when Spotify deprecated Audio Features in Nov 2024. Chosic caps free analysis at 1,000 songs, while Skiley and Playlistation require paid subs and spam your sidebar with static playlists based on coarse artist genres. Marvis Pro (~$10) is iOS + Apple Music only. Record Club requires manual album logging.
• Manual Sorting (Folders / Notion): sorting 3,600 tracks at 10 sec/track takes 10 hours of manual desktop drag-and-drop + 30 min/week maintenance.

Operational, not informational problem: cannot be solved by Googling or prompting ChatGPT (directly passes our mentor's filter).
Low direct competition in 2026: Spotify's API changes killed legacy free tools (SmarterPlaylists), leaving a clear market gap.
Strong local angle: Spotify's basic Liked Songs genre filters aren't even rolled out in Moldova.
Easy Midterm 2 validation: finding 15–20 university students with 2,000+ liked songs for video interviews is super easy.
Buildable Core: DB schema, album backlog kanban, boolean query engine, true stratified shuffle, and LLM Text-to-Filter over tagged metadata are straightforward to build.

Solution Proposal

A web-based discovery platform that interfaces with embedded streaming audio (via the YouTube IFrame API) to highlight, describe, and recommend

rather than full compositions.

The core user flow is as follows: The user loads a track (via curated recommendation, search, or random discovery). Through a Segmented Waveform Visualizer, the track timeline is broken into distinct, highlighted passages (typically 4–30 seconds in length). Clicking an active passage displays its descriptive tags (e.g.,

). The user selects the specific elements they want to explore. The platform returns a ranked feed of related musical passages across diverse catalog tracks that match those specific descriptors. Clicking a recommended result immediately jumps the built-in player to that exact timestamp and activates an automatic loop over the passage window.

This system eliminates the tedious, manual playback scrubbing and directly targets the creative moments producers actually want to manipulate, thus significantly accelerating the sampling workflow.

The shift toward AI-driven automated tagging is not merely a whim of the developers at Cyanite; it is a solution to major challenges in the music industry—tasks that humans simply cannot handle effectively. Creators often evaluate their own tracks based on personal emotion, which rarely aligns with how potential buyers—such as music editors, directors, or content creators—actually search for music. 
Furthermore, you still haven’t explained how you intend to moderate the tags applied by users. The perception of music is deeply subjective; what one person might label "aggressive rock," another could interpret as "energetic alternative pop." This creates a significant problem: if a user tries to search for samples using a specific combination of tags, they might end up with completely nonsensical results, simply because everyone interprets those tags differently. It’s impossible to find moderators who could meticulously verify whether every tag has been applied correctly—and even if you could, it wouldn’t solve the issue, as moderators are, after all, only human, and their own perceptions would vary just as much.

Each day, he dedicates 1-1.5 hours to crate-digging through obscure 1970s Japanese jazz-fusion and MPB recordings on YouTube and Samplette.
”I find this amazing sample from a Masayoshi Takanaka song on YouTube and it's like a background vocal, and I want to accompany it with an acoustic guitar or something mellow. 
After listening to about 5-6 more recommended jazz-fusion tracks that last 4-8 min in length, I still feel like something is missing, like none of what I listened to has guitars
used in the way I want them. The first sample doesn't work only by itself, and I don't have any saved guitar samples that fit, but I spent almost half an hour on this and I need to start on my homework soon.
I just don't have the time to finish this idea."
Alex has a clear goal: he wants to mix a high-quality sample with an ideal instrumental section from an underground track, but he has limited time to search for these samples,
leaving him feel dissatisfied when he listens to song after song without any useful material found.

Annie Lee (20, Hobbyist SoundCloud Producer). Annie is a FAF student at UTM and uses time during weekends to experiment with sound-design and improve at mixing and mastering. 
Before using the plugins she set up for the Mixer channels in her FL Studio project, she first needs a collection of samples to test it on. 
"I usually look up sounds on Splice to play around with, like instruments or sound effects, but I feel like I explored all the options I could find available, and most of the other ones
I find are pretty bland. If I look something up online, its hard to find any usable music because most of it just sounds generic and uninspired. Samplette is pretty good for finding niche
music, but all of it is random and I don't know what I'm looking for when I listen to these. Sometimes I stumble upon something fun to work with, but its quite rare and I don't know how
to find more stuff like it."
Annie finds it monotonous to look up full songs on the internet due to the inability of specifying audio-level requests on the websites she uses. Even when given filters, finding samples
in the same style is difficult to define without more proper information, so useful material comes much more rarely than she would prefer.

text:
Quick summary for everyone on what our project (Sample Browser) actually is now and how it works for a producer:

THE PROBLEM:

text.text: When music producers look for samples in full songs on YouTube or Samplette, they don't need the whole 5-minute song — they just need a clean 10-second part (for example, a piano intro without vocals, or a clean drum break). Right now, platforms only tag the whole song, so producers waste a lot of time manually skipping through dozens of videos to find those short clean sections, and have no easy way to save exact timestamps for later.

text: OUR SOLUTION (Sample Browser):

text.text:
It’s a website built on top of the embedded YouTube player. We DO NOT download or process any audio/video with AI — our database only stores YouTube links, start/end timestamps (like 1:15–1:25), and tags.

WHAT A PRODUCER CAN DO ON THE SITE:
1. See highlighted sections inside a song:
When you open a song, you see colored blocks on the timeline (e.g., 0:00–0:14 [Intro | Rhodes Piano | No Drums]). You click a block, and the YouTube player immediately jumps to that exact second and loops that short section on repeat so you can hear if it works as a sample.

2. Find similar sample sections across other songs:
While listening to a section you like, you can click its tags (for example, [Guitar] + [No Vocals] + [Break]) and the site shows you a list of other songs that have the exact same tags — and when you click them, it jumps straight to that specific timestamp in the new song, not the beginning of the video.

3. Save and tag sections for yourself (or share them):
When you find a cool 10-second moment in a YouTube video, you can mark the Start and End time, pick preset tags in 2–3 clicks (what instrument is playing, whether there are vocals/drums, what part of the song it is), and save it to your personal online library ("Cloud Crate") so you don't have to download the whole file or forget which second of the video had the sample.

text: WHY WE USE TWO TYPES OF TAGS:

text.text:
- Main Preset Tags (objective facts everyone agrees on): Instrument ([Piano], [Guitar], [Bass]), Isolation ([No Vocals], [No Drums], [Solo]), and Song Part ([Intro], [Break], [Outro]).
- Secondary Tags (optional mood/style words like [Dusty] or [Dark]): these have lower priority, and since you can instantly play the 10-second loop in 1 click, you immediately hear what the tag means.

text: The approach to labeling samples has been revised. We have completely moved away from local analysis of recordings (which required prior downloading) to address issues related to YouTube’s terms of service. Furthermore, we have categorized tags into subjective and objective types—with the latter further subdivided into several groups for the convenience of those creating the labels—to ensure that different contributors do not get confused by each other’s annotations.
